nodes.name: Sobolev space $\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$
nodes.statement: Aside from the space  $L^2(\Omega_r)$ of square-integrable functions on $\Omega_r$, we also need the Sobolev space $\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s\geq 0$. It is defined by \begin{align} \mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)=\left\{F\in L^2(\Omega_r):\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)}^2=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\Big(n+\textnormal{\footnotesize $\frac{1}{2}$}\Big)^{2s} \big|F_r^\wedge(n,k)\big|^2<\infty\right\}, \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Sobolev space of $L^2(\Omega_r)$ functions whose Fourier coefficients decay fast enough that the $(n+\frac{1}{2})^{2s}$-weighted energy is finite.

nodes.name: Fourier coefficient $F_r^\wedge(n,k)$
nodes.statement: where $F_r^\wedge(n,k)$ denotes the Fourier coefficient of degree $n$ and order $k$, i.e., \begin{align} F_r^\wedge(n,k)=\int_{\Omega_r}F(y)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\left(\frac{y}{|y|}\right)d\omega(y). \end{align}
nodes.genus: Fourier coefficient of degree $n$ and order $k$

nodes.name: $\textnormal{Pol}_{N}$, space of band-limited zonal kernels
nodes.statement: A further notion that we need is \begin{align} \textnormal{Pol}_{N}=\left\{K(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}K^\wedge(n) Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)Y_{n,k}\left(\eta\right):K^\wedge(n)\in\mathbb{R}\right\}, \end{align} the space of all band-limited zonal kernels with maximal degree $N$ (as always, $\xi$, $\eta$ denote the unit vectors $\frac{x}{|x|}$ and $\frac{y}{|y|}$, respectively).
nodes.statement_short: Space of zonal kernels expandable in spherical harmonics up to degree $N$ with real symbols.
nodes.genus: space of all band-limited zonal kernels

nodes.name: zonal kernel
nodes.statement: Zonal means that $K$ only depends on the scalar product $\xi\cdot\eta$, more precisely, \begin{align} K(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{2n+1}{4\pi}K^\wedge(n) P_n\left(\xi\cdot\eta\right), \end{align} with $P_n$ being the Legendre polynomial of degree $n$ (the expressions \eqref{polnj1} and \eqref{eqn:Kzonal} are connected by the spherical addition theorem). Thus, instead of $K(\cdot,\cdot)$ acting on $\Omega_r\times\Omega_R$ or $\Omega_r\times\Omega_r$, it can also be regarded as a function $K(\cdot)$ acting on the interval $[-1,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: A kernel is zonal when it depends only on $\xi\cdot\eta$, hence is a Legendre expansion on $[-1,1]$.
differentia: only depends on the scalar product $\xi\cdot\eta$

nodes.name: upward continuation operator $T^{up}$
nodes.statement: Opposed to this, the determination of $F_1$ from $U^+$ is known as upward continuation. The operator $T^{up}:L^2(\Omega_r)\to L^2(\Omega_R)$, given by \begin{align} F_1(x)={T}^{up}[U^+](x)=\int_{\Omega_r}K^{up}(x,y) U^+(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\Omega_R, \end{align} with \begin{align} K^{up}(x,y)&=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\sigma_n\frac{1}{R}Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\left(\eta\right) \end{align} and $\sigma_n=\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^n$, describes this process.
nodes.statement_short: Upward continuation maps a potential on $\Omega_r$ to $\Omega_R$ by convolution with the kernel whose symbols are $\sigma_n=(r/R)^n$.

nodes.name: downward continuation operator $T^{down}$
nodes.statement: The downward continuation operator $T^{down}$ and acts in the following way: \begin{align} U^+(x)={T}^{down}[F_1](x)=\int_{\Omega_R}K^{down}(x,y) U^+(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\Omega_r, \end{align} with \begin{align} K^{down}(x,y)&=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\frac{1}{\sigma_n}\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\frac{1}{R}Y_{n,k}\left(\eta\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Downward continuation is the (unbounded) inverse convolution operator with amplifying symbols $1/\sigma_n$.

nodes.name: scaling kernel $\Phi_N$
nodes.statement: $T_N$ reflects a regularized version of the downward continuation operator, acting as a scaling transform on $\Omega_R$ with the convolution kernel \begin{align} {\Phi_N(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^N\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\frac{1}{R}Y_{n,k}\left(\eta\right).} \end{align} We frequently use $\xi$ and $\eta$ to abbreviate the unit vectors $\frac{x}{|x|}$ and $\frac{y}{|y|}$, respectively, and write $r=|x|$, $R=|y|$. Furthermore, $\{Y_{n,k}\}_{n=0,1,\ldots;k=1,\ldots,2n+1}$ denotes a set of orthonormal spherical harmonics of degree $n$ and order $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Band-limited scaling kernel of degree $N$ with symbols $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)$, mapping $\Omega_R$ to $\Omega_r$.
differentia: acting as a scaling transform on $\Omega_R$

nodes.name: wavelet kernel $\tilde{\Psi}_N$
nodes.statement: In order to refine the approximation with local data we use the operator $\tilde{W}_N$, which acts as a wavelet transform on $\Gamma_r$ with the convolution kernel \begin{align} {\tilde{\Psi}_N(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\left(\eta\right), } \end{align} where $\kappa>1$ is a fixed constant (reflecting the higher resolution desired for the refinement). The coefficients ${\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)$ are typically called 'symbols' of the corresponding kernels.
nodes.statement_short: Band-limited wavelet kernel of degree $\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$ acting on $\Gamma_r$, used for the local refinement step.
differentia: acts as a wavelet transform on $\Gamma_r$

nodes.name: bounded scaling transform $T_N$
nodes.statement: The bounded scaling transform $T_N:L^2(\Omega_R)\to L^2(\Omega_r)$ is then defined via \begin{align} {{T}_N[F_1](x)=\int_{\Omega_R}\Phi_N(x,y) F_1(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\Omega_r,} \end{align} and represents an approximation of $T^{down}[F_1]$.

nodes.name: wavelet transform $W_N$
nodes.statement: This operator can be refined further by use of the wavelet transform \begin{align} {W}_N[F_1](x)=\int_{\Omega_R}\Psi_N(x,y) F_1(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\Omega_r, \end{align} where the kernel $\Psi_N$ is of the form \eqref{eqn:psin} with symbols $\Psi_N^\wedge(n)=\Phi_{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}^\wedge(n)-\Phi_N^\wedge(n)$.

nodes.name: spherical cap $\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho)$ and the subregion $\tilde{\Gamma}_r$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho)$ denotes the spherical cap $\{y\in\Omega_r:1-\frac{x}{|x|}\cdot\frac{y}{|y|}<\rho\}$ with radius $\rho\in(0,2)$ and center $x\in\Omega_r$. The subset $\tilde{\Gamma}_r\subset\Gamma_r$ is chosen such that $\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho)\subset\Gamma_r$ for every $x\in\tilde{\Gamma}_r$ and some $\rho\in(0,2)$ that is fixed in advance.
nodes.section: 2.2 Combination of Downward Continuation and Local Data

nodes.name: local wavelet transform $\tilde{W}_N$
nodes.statement: Remembering that $F_2$ is only available locally in $\Gamma_r$ and paying tribute to \eqref{eqn:Wjrr}, we define the wavelet transform \begin{align} {\tilde{W}_N[F_2](x)=\int_{\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho)}\tilde{\Psi}_N(x,y) F_2(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\tilde{\Gamma}_r.} \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.2 Combination of Downward Continuation and Local Data

nodes.name: Shannon-type kernels $\Phi_N^{Sh}$, $\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}$
nodes.statement: As an auxiliary set of kernels, we define the Shannon-type kernels $\Phi_N^{Sh}$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}$ via the symbols \begin{align} \big(\Phi_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{1}{\sigma_n},&n\leq N,\\0,&\textnormal{else},\end{array}\right.\qquad \big(\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}1,&n\leq \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor,\\0,&\textnormal{else},\end{array}\right. \end{align} and $\big(\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=\big(\tilde{\Phi}_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)-\big(\Phi_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$. $\Phi_N^{Sh}$ represents the kernel of the so-called truncated singular value decomposition for the downward continuation operator ${T}^{down}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hard-truncated (Shannon) reference kernels; $\Phi_N^{Sh}$ is the TSVD kernel of $T^{down}$.

nodes.name: vector spherical harmonics ${y}_{n,k}^{(i)}$
nodes.statement: Before dealing with the actual problem, it is necessary to introduce some basic vectorial framework. Here, we mainly follow the course of \cite{freeschrei09} and use the following set of vector spherical harmonics: \begin{align} {y}_{n,k}^{(1)}\left(\xi\right)&=\xi Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right), \\{y}_{n,k}^{(2)}\left(\xi\right)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n+1)}}\nabla^*_{\xi}Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right), \\{y}_{n,k}^{(3)}\left(\xi\right)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n+1)}}L_{\xi}^*Y_{n,k}\left(\xi\right), \end{align} for $n=1,2,\ldots$, and $k=1,\ldots, 2n+1$, with ${y}_{n,k}^{(1)}$ additionally being defined for $n=0$ and $k=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Radial, surface-gradient, and surface-curl vector spherical harmonics forming an orthonormal basis of $l^2(\Omega)$.

nodes.name: tensorial Legendre polynomials $\mathbf{P}^{(i,i)}_n$
nodes.statement: They are complemented by a set of tensorial Legendre polynomials $\mathbf{P}^{(i,i)}_n$ of degree $n$ and type $(i,i)$ that are defined via \begin{align} \mathbf{P}^{(1,1)}_n\left(\xi,\eta\right)&=\xi\otimes\eta \,P_n\left(\xi\cdot\eta\right), \\\mathbf{P}^{(2,2)}_n\left(\xi,\eta\right)&=\frac{1}{{n(n+1)}}\nabla^*_{\xi}\otimes\nabla^*_{\eta}P_n\left(\xi\cdot\eta\right), \\\mathbf{P}^{(3,3)}_n\left(\xi,\eta\right)&=\frac{1}{{n(n+1)}}L^*_{\xi}\otimes L^*_{\eta}P_n\left(\xi\cdot\eta\right). \end{align} The operator $\otimes$ denotes the tensor product $x\otimes y=xy^T$ of two vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^3$.
nodes.genus: set of tensorial Legendre polynomials of degree $n$ and type $(i,i)$

nodes.name: vectorial Sobolev space $\mathfrak{h}_s(\Omega_r)$
nodes.statement: The vectorial counterpart to the Sobolev space $\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$ is defined as \begin{align} \mathfrak{h}_s(\Omega_r)=\Big\{f\in l^2(\Omega_r) :\|f\|_{\mathfrak{h}_s(\Omega_r)}^2=\sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{n=0_i}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\left(n+\textnormal{\footnotesize$\frac{1}{2}$}\right)^{2s}\big|({f}_r^{(i)})^\wedge(n,k)\big|^2<\infty\Big\}, \end{align} where $0_i=0$ if $i=1$ and $0_i=1$ if $i=2$, and $({f}_r^{(i)})^\wedge(n,k)$ denotes the Fourier coefficient of degree $n$, order $k$, and type $i$, i.e., \begin{align} ({f}_r^{(i)})^\wedge(n,k)=\int_{\Omega_r}f(y)\cdot \frac{1}{r}y_{n,k}^{(i)}\left(\frac{y}{|y|}\right)d\omega(y). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Vectorial Sobolev space of $l^2(\Omega_r)$ fields with finite $(n+\frac{1}{2})^{2s}$-weighted type-$i$ Fourier energy.
nodes.genus: vectorial counterpart to the Sobolev space $\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$

nodes.name: $\mathbf{Pol}_{N}$, space of band-limited tensorial kernels
nodes.statement: The space of band-limited tensorial kernels with maximal degree $N$ is defined as \begin{align} \mathbf{Pol}_{N}=\left\{\mathbf{K}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{n=0_i}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\mathbf{K}^\wedge(n) {y}^{(i)}_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\otimes{y}^{(i)}_{n,k}\left(\eta\right):\mathbf{K}^\wedge(n)\in\mathbb{R}\right\}. \end{align} The kernels $\mathbf{Pol}_{N}$ are tensor-zonal. In particular, this means that the absolute value $|{\mathbf{K}}(x,y)|$ depends only on the scalar product $\xi\cdot\eta$ (this does not have to hold true for the kernel ${\mathbf{K}}(x,y)$ itself).
nodes.statement_short: Tensor-zonal analogue of $\textnormal{Pol}_N$, built from tensor products of vector spherical harmonics up to degree $N$.

nodes.name: vectorial scaling transform $t_N$ with tensorial scaling kernel $\mathbf{\Phi}_N$
nodes.statement: Similar to the scalar case in Subsection \ref{subsec:dc}, there is a vectorial upward continuation operator $t^{up}$ and a vectorial downward continuation operator $t^{down}$, defined via tensorial kernels with singular values $\sigma_n=\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^{n+1}$ and $\frac{1}{\sigma_n}$, respectively (note that in the scalar case, $\sigma_n=\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^{n}$). The downward continuation operator can be approximated by a bounded operator $t_N:l^2(\Omega_R)\to l^2(\Omega_r)$: \begin{align} {t_N[f_1](x)=\int_{\Omega_R}\mathbf{\Phi}_N(x,y) f_1(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\Omega_r,} \end{align} with \begin{align} {\mathbf{\Phi}_N(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{n=0_i}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\mathbf{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\frac{1}{r}{y}^{(i)}_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\otimes \frac{1}{R}{y}^{(i)}_{n,k}\left(\eta\right).} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bounded vectorial scaling transform approximating $t^{down}$, with tensorial kernel $\mathbf{\Phi}_N$ and singular values $\sigma_n=(r/R)^{n+1}$.
nodes.genus: bounded operator approximating the vectorial downward continuation operator $t^{down}$

nodes.name: vectorial wavelet operator $\tilde{{w}}_N$ with tensorial wavelet kernel $\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N$
nodes.statement: A refinement by local data in $\Gamma_r$ is achieved by the vectorial wavelet operator $\tilde{{w}}_N:l^2({\Gamma}_r)\to l^2(\tilde{\Gamma}_r)$: \begin{align} {\tilde{{w}}_N[f_2](x)=\int_{\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho)}\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N(x,y) f_2(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\tilde{\Gamma}_r,} \end{align} with \begin{align} {\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{n=0_i}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\tilde{ \mathbf{\Psi}}_{N}^\wedge(n)\frac{1}{r}{y}^{(i)}_{n,k}\left(\xi\right)\otimes \frac{1}{r}{y}^{(i)}_{n,k}\left(\eta\right)}, \end{align} for some fixed $\kappa>1$, and \begin{align} {\tilde{ \mathbf{\Psi}}_{N}^\wedge(n)=\tilde{ \mathbf{\Phi}}_{N}^\wedge(n)-\mathbf{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\sigma_n.} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Vectorial local wavelet operator on spherical caps, with tensorial wavelet kernel coupled to $\mathbf{\Phi}_N$ by $\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge=\tilde{\mathbf{\Phi}}_N^\wedge-\mathbf{\Phi}_N^\wedge\sigma_n$.

nodes.name: surface gradient $\nabla^*_\xi$ and surface curl gradient $L^*_{\xi}$
nodes.statement:
The operator $
abla^*_\xi$ denotes the surface gradient, i.e., the tangential contribution of the gradient $
abla_x$ (more precisely, $
abla_x=\xi rac{\partial}{\partial{r}}+ rac{1}{r}
abla^*_{\xi}$, with $\xi= rac{x}{|x|}$ and $r=|x|$). The surface curl gradient $L^*_{\xi}$ stands short for $\xi\wedge
abla_{\xi}^*$ (with $\wedge$ being the vector product of two vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^3$).
nodes.definiendum: surface gradient $\nabla^*_\xi$ and surface curl gradient $L^*_{\xi}$
nodes.genus: tangential differential operators on the sphere

nodes.name: Conditions (a), (b) on the scaling symbols $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)$
nodes.statement: Following the course of \cite{freeden99} and \cite{schneider98}, we assume $\Phi_N$ to be a scaling kernel of the form \eqref{eqn:phin} with truncation index $\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$ and symbols $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)$ that satisfy \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $\lim_{N\to\infty}\Phi_N^\wedge(n)=\frac{1}{\sigma_n}$, uniformly with respect to $n=0,1,\ldots$, \item[(b)] $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{2n+1}{4\pi} \big|\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\big|< \infty$,  for all $N=0,1,\ldots$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Scaling symbols must converge uniformly to $1/\sigma_n$ and be absolutely summable for each $N$.

nodes.name: Conditions (a'), (b') on the auxiliary symbols $\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)$
nodes.statement: The auxiliary symbol needs to satisfy \begin{itemize} \item[(a')] $\lim_{N\to\infty}\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)=1$, uniformly with respect to $n=0,1,\ldots$, \item[(b')] $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{2n+1}{4\pi} \big|\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)\big|< \infty$,  for all $N=0,1,\ldots$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Auxiliary symbols must converge uniformly to $1$ and be absolutely summable for each $N$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Combination of Downward Continuation and Local Data

nodes.name: Deterministic noise model for the input data
nodes.statement: From now on we assume contaminated input data $F_1^{\eps_1}=F_1+\eps_1E_1$ and $F_2^{\varepsilon_2}=F_2+\varepsilon_2E_2$ with deterministic noise $E_1\in L^2(\Omega_R)$, $E_2\in L^2(\Omega_r)$, and $\eps_1,\eps_2>0$.

nodes.name: Vectorial symbol conditions and vectorial noise model
nodes.statement: The symbols $\mathbf{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)$ need to satisfy the same conditions (a), (b) as for the scalar analogue in Subsection \ref{subsec:dc}. [...] The symbols $\tilde{ \mathbf{\Phi}}_{N}^\wedge(n)$ are assumed to satisfy conditions $($a'$)$ and $($b'$)$ from Subsection \ref{subsec:comb}. As in the scalar case, the input data $f_1$, $f_2$ is perturbed by deterministic noise $e_1\in l^2(\Omega_R)$ and $e_2\in l^2(\Omega_r)$, so that we are dealing with $f_1^{\eps_1}=f_1+\eps_1 e_1$ and $f_2^{\eps_2}=f_2+\eps_2 e_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Vectorial symbols obey the same conditions (a),(b),(a'),(b') as in the scalar case, with deterministic vectorial noise.

nodes.name: Combined downward-continuation / local-data boundary-value problem
nodes.statement: From satellite measurements we obtain data $F_1$ on a spherical orbit $\Omega_R=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|=R\}$ and from ground or near-ground measurements data $F_2$ in a subregion $\Gamma_r$ of the spherical Earth surface $\Omega_r$ of radius $r<R$ (cf. Figure \ref{fig:datasit}). The problem to solve is \begin{align} \Delta U=0,\quad&\textnormal{ in }\Omega_r^{ext}, \\U=F_1,\quad&\textnormal{ on }\Omega_R, \\U=F_2,\quad&\textnormal{ on }\Gamma_r, \end{align} with $\Omega_r^{ext}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|>r\}$ denoting the space exterior to the sphere $\Omega_r$. Of interest to us is the restriction $U^+=U|_{\Gamma_r}$, i.e., the potential in the subregion $\Gamma_r$ of the Earth's surface.
nodes.statement_short: Recover a harmonic potential on a local patch of the Earth's surface from global satellite data plus local ground data.

nodes.name: Minimization of the functional $\mathcal{F}(\Phi_N,\tilde{\Psi}_N)$
nodes.statement: Eventually, finding 'good' kernels $\Phi_N$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ reduces to finding symbols $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)$, $\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)$ that keep the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:errorestfinal} small (note that $\tilde{\Psi}_{N}^\wedge(n)$ is given by $\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)-\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$). We choose these symbols to be the minimizers of the functional \begin{equation} {\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}(\Phi_N,\tilde{\Psi}_N)=&\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\big|1-\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\big|^2+\sum_{n=0}^{N}\alpha_{N,n}\big|1-{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\sigma_n\big|^2 \\&+\beta_N\sum_{n=0}^{N}\big|\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\big|^2+8\pi^2 r^4\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\big\|^2_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}, \end{aligned}} \end{equation} with $\Phi_N$ being a member of Pol$_{N}$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ a member of Pol$_{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the kernel symbols by minimizing a four-term functional balancing approximation error, downward-continuation error, operator norm, and spatial leakage.

nodes.name: Vectorial boundary-value problem for $b=\nabla U$
nodes.statement:
In some geophysical problems, especially in geomagnetism, it is not the scalar potential $U$ we are interested in but the vectorial gradient $
abla U$. Just as well, it is often the gradient $
abla U$ that is measured on $\Omega_R$ and $\Gamma_r$. Thus, we are not confronted with the scalar equations \eqref{eqn:11}--\eqref{eqn:13} but with the vectorial problem  egin{align} b=
abla U,&\quad 	extnormal{in }\Omega_r^{ext}, \\Delta U=0,&\quad 	extnormal{in }\Omega_r^{ext}, \b=f_1,&\quad 	extnormal{on }\Omega_R, \b=f_2,&\quad 	extnormal{on }\Gamma_r. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Vectorial version of the problem: recover $b=\nabla U$ on $\Gamma_r$ from vectorial data on $\Omega_R$ and $\Gamma_r$.

nodes.name: Minimization of the vectorial functional $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{\Phi}_N,\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N)$
nodes.statement: A similar error estimate as in \eqref{eqn:errorestfinal} motivates the minimization of the functional \begin{equation} {\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{\Phi}_N,\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N)=&\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\big|1-\tilde{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{N}^\wedge(n)\big|^2+\sum_{n=0}^{N}\alpha_{N,n}\big|1-{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{N}^\wedge(n)\sigma_n\big|^2 \\&+\beta_N\sum_{n=0}^{N}\big|\mathbf{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)\big|^2+8\pi^2 r^4\big\|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\big\|^2_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}. \end{aligned}} \end{equation} In the vectorial case, the term $\|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\|^2_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}$ is not quite as basic as in the scalar case \eqref{eqn:1dint} but still expressible by elementary means.
nodes.statement_short: Vectorial kernel-design functional, structurally identical to the scalar one with tensorial symbols.

nodes.name: Two-step approximation $U_N={T}_N[F_1]+{\tilde{W}}_N[F_2]$
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we use an approximation $U_N$ of $U^+$ of the form \begin{align} {U_N={T}_N[F_1]+{\tilde{W}}_N[F_2].} \end{align} It is motivated by spherical multiscale representations as introduced in \cite{schneider98} and \cite{freewind}
nodes.statement_short: The approximation is a scaling transform of satellite data plus a local wavelet transform of ground data.

nodes.name: Symbol coupling $\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)=\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)-\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$
nodes.statement: We slightly modify the symbol $\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)$ by use of the auxiliary symbol $\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)$, so that it reads  \begin{align} {\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)=\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)-\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n.} \end{align} This has the effect that now two parameters are available, namely $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)$, which reflects the behaviour of the operator $T_N$ responsible for the downward continuation, and $\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)$, which offers a chance to control the localization of $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ and the behaviour of $\tilde{W}_N$ to a certain amount.
nodes.statement_short: Coupling the wavelet symbol to an auxiliary symbol decouples downward-continuation control from localization control.
nodes.section: 2.2 Combination of Downward Continuation and Local Data

nodes.name: Multiscale refinement ${T}_{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}={T}_N+W_N$
nodes.statement: An approximation of $T^{down}[F_1]$ at the higher scale $\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$, for some fixed $\kappa>1$, is then given by \begin{align} {T}_{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}[F_1](x)={T}_N[F_1](x)+W_N[F_1](x),\quad x\in\Omega_r. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Scaling at scale $\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$ equals scaling at scale $N$ plus the wavelet correction.

nodes.name: Transfer of the wavelet transform from $\Omega_R$ to $\Omega_r$
nodes.statement: In order to incorporate data $F_2$ in $\Gamma_r$ by use of a wavelet transform, it is necessary to rewrite \eqref{eqn:WjRr}. Observing that $F_1$ and $F_2$ are only specific expressions of $U$ on the spheres $\Omega_R$ and $\Omega_r$, respectively, we find \begin{align} &\int_{\Omega_R}\Psi_N(x,y) F_1(y)d\omega(y)=\int_{\Omega_R}\Psi_N(x,y) U(y)d\omega(y) \\&=\int_{\Omega_r}\tilde{\Psi}_N(x,y) U(y)d\omega(y)=\int_{\Omega_r}\tilde{\Psi}_N(x,y) F_2(y)d\omega(y),\quad x\in\Omega_r,\nonumber \end{align} where $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ is of the form \eqref{eqn:psin} with  $\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)=\sigma_n{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)=\Phi_{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}^\wedge(n)\sigma_n-\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$ (the factor $\sigma_n$ stems from the downward continuation that occurs in the second equality of \eqref{eqn:Wjrr}).
nodes.statement_short: The wavelet correction computed from satellite data equals a wavelet convolution of the ground data, at the cost of a factor $\sigma_n$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Combination of Downward Continuation and Local Data

nodes.name: Noisy approximation $U_N^\eps$
nodes.statement: The approximation \eqref{eqn:firstapprox2} of $U^+$ in $\tilde{\Gamma}_r$ is then modified by \begin{align} {U_N^\eps={T}_N[F_1^{\eps_1}]+{\tilde{W}}_N[F_2^{\eps_2}],} \end{align} where $\eps$ stands short for $(\eps_1,\eps_2)^T$.

nodes.name: Overall error estimate for $\|U^+ - U_N^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^2(\tilde{\Gamma}_r)}$
nodes.statement_short: Total error is bounded by two symbol-approximation terms, two noise-amplification terms, and one localization-leakage term.

nodes.name: Slepian-type localization ratio for $\tilde{\Psi}_N$
nodes.statement: While we have used $\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}$ as a measure for the localization inside a spherical cap $\mathcal{C}_r(\cdot,\rho)$ (values close to zero meaning a good localization, i.e., small leakage of information into $\Omega_r\setminus\mathcal{C}_r(\cdot,\rho)$), a more suitable quantity to consider would be \begin{align} \frac{\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\big\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}}{\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\big\|_{L^2([-1,1])}}. \end{align} This is essentially the expression that is minimized for the construction of Slepian functions (see, e.g., \cite{plattner13}, \cite{plattner13b}, \cite{simons06}, \cite{simons10}).
nodes.statement_short: The relative energy outside the cap is the Slepian-style localization measure.

nodes.name: Vectorial approximation $b_N^{\eps}={t}_{N}[f_1^{\eps_1}]+\tilde{{w}}_{N}[f_2^{\eps_2}]$
nodes.statement: An approximation of $b^+$ in $\tilde{\Gamma}_r$ is then defined by \begin{align} {b_N^{\eps}={t}_{N}[f_1^{\eps_1}]+\tilde{{w}}_{N}[f_2^{\eps_2}].} \end{align}

nodes.name: Legendre recurrence relation
nodes.statement: First, we use the addition theorem for spherical harmonics and the recurrence relation  $tP_n(t)=\frac{1}{2n+1}\left((n+1)P_{n+1}(t)+nP_{n-1}(t)\right)$ to obtain

nodes.name: Legendre differential equation
nodes.statement: Observing the differential equation $(1-t^2)P_n''(t)-2tP_n'(t)+n(n+1)P_n(t)=0$, $t\in[-1,1]$, for Legendre polynomials leads to

nodes.name: Surface curl gradient identity $L_{\xi}^*P_{n}=-L_{\eta}^*P_{n}$
nodes.statement: The surface curl gradient has the nice property $L_{\xi}^*P_{n}\left(\xi\cdot\eta\right)=-L_{\eta}^*P_{n}\left(\xi\cdot\eta\right)$ which we have used in the seventh line of Equation \eqref{eqn:shit}.

nodes.name: Decomposition $f(x)=\xi F_1(x)+\nabla^*_\xi F_2(x)$
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is of class $\mathfrak{h}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s\geq 2$, it follows that $f(x)=\xi F_1(x)+\nabla^*_\xi F_2(x)$ for some scalar functions $F_1$ of class $\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$ and $F_2$ of class $\mathcal{H}_{s+1}(\Omega_r)$.
nodes.statement_short: A type-$(1,2)$ vector field splits into a radial and a surface-gradient part with scalar Sobolev potentials.

nodes.name: One-dimensional localization integral $\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_{N}\big\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}^2$
nodes.statement: For the last estimate on the right hand side, we observe that, due to the zonality of the kernels, $\sup_{x\in\Omega_r}\|\tilde{\Psi}_{N}(x,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\Omega_r\setminus\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho))}$ coincides with $\sqrt{2\pi} r\|\tilde{\Psi}_{N}\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}$, where \begin{align} \big\|\tilde{\Psi}_{N}\big\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}^2=\int_{-1}^{1-\rho}|\tilde{\Psi}_{N}(t)|^2dt. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Zonality reduces the leakage norm outside the cap to a one-dimensional integral independent of $x$.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.1 (unique minimizers of $\mathcal{F}$ solve a linear system)
nodes.statement: Assume that all parameters $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$, $\alpha_{N,n}$, and $\beta_N$ are positive. Then there exist unique minimizers $\Phi_N\in\textnormal{Pol}_{N}$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N\in\textnormal{Pol}_{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}$ of the functional $\mathcal{F}$ in \eqref{eqn:mineq2} that are determined by the symbols $\phi=(\Phi_N^\wedge(1)\sigma_1,\ldots,\Phi_N^\wedge(N)\sigma_{N},\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(1),\ldots,\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor))^T$ which solve the linear equations \begin{align} \mathbf{M}\phi=\alpha, \end{align} where \begin{align} \mathbf{M}=\left(\begin{array}{c|c}\mathbf{D}_1+\mathbf{P}_1&-\mathbf{P}_2\\\hline-\mathbf{P}_3&\mathbf{D}_2+\mathbf{P}_4\end{array}\right), \end{align} and $\alpha=(\alpha_{N,1},\ldots,\alpha_{N,N},\tilde{\alpha}_{N,1},\ldots,\tilde{\alpha}_{N,\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor})^T$. The diagonal matrices $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$ are given by \begin{align} \mathbf{D}_1=\textnormal{diag}\left(\frac{\beta_N}{\sigma_n^2}+\alpha_{N,n}\right)_{n=0,\ldots,N}, \qquad\mathbf{D}_2=\textnormal{diag}\big(\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\big)_{n=0,\ldots,\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}, \end{align} whereas $\mathbf{P}_1$,\ldots, $\mathbf{P}_4$ are submatrices of the Gram matrix $\big(P_{n,m}^\rho\big)_{n,m=0,\ldots, \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}$. More precisely, \begin{align} \mathbf{P}_1=\big(P_{n,m}^\rho\big)_{n,m=0,\ldots,N},&\qquad \mathbf{P}_2=\big(P_{n,m}^\rho\big)_{n=0,\ldots,N\atop m=0,\ldots,\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}, \\\mathbf{P}_3=\big(P_{n,m}^\rho\big)_{n=0,\ldots,\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor\atop m=0,\ldots,N},&\qquad\mathbf{P}_4=\big(P_{n,m}^\rho\big)_{n,m=0,\ldots,\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}. \end{align} with \begin{align} P_{n,m}^\rho=\frac{(2n+1)(2m+1)}{2}\int_{-1}^{1-\rho}P_n(t)P_m(t)dt. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: For positive parameters the optimal symbols exist, are unique, and are the solution of a block linear system built from diagonal and Gram matrices.

nodes.name: Proposition 4.2 (Riemann localization for the Shannon-type kernel)
nodes.statement: If $F\in\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s\geq 2$, it holds that \begin{align} \lim_{N\to\infty}\left\|\int_{\Omega_r\setminus\mathcal{C}_r(\rho,\cdot)}\tilde{\Psi}^{Sh}_N(\cdot,y)F(y)d\omega(y)\right\|_{L^2 (\Omega_r)}=0, \end{align} where $\tilde{\Psi}^{Sh}_N$ is the Shannon-type kernel with symbols $\big(\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=1$, if $N +1\leq n\leq \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$, and $\big(\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=0$, else.
nodes.statement_short: For smooth enough $F$, the Shannon-type wavelet convolution over the complement of the cap vanishes as $N\to\infty$.
assumptions: If $F\in\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s\geq 2$
conclusions: $\lim_{N\to\infty}\left\|\int_{\Omega_r\setminus\mathcal{C}_r(\rho,\cdot)}\tilde{\Psi}^{Sh}_N(\cdot,y)F(y)d\omega(y)\right\|_{L^2 (\Omega_r)}=0$
nodes.origin_citation: Wang, Sloan & Womersley 2013 (Dirichlet Kernel for the Sphere)

nodes.name: Theorem 4.3 (convergence of $U_N^\varepsilon$)
nodes.statement: Assume that the parameters $\alpha_{N,n}$, $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$, and $\beta_N$ are positive and suppose that, for some fixed $\delta>0$ and $\kappa>1$, \begin{align} \inf_{n=0,\ldots, \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\frac{\beta_N\frac{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2(N+1)}}{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^2}+( \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor+1)^2}{{\alpha}_{N,n}}&=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-2(1+\delta)}\right),\quad \textit{ for }N\to\infty. \end{align} The same relation shall hold true for $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$. Additionally, let every $N$ be associated with an $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_1(N)>0$ and an $\varepsilon_2=\varepsilon_2(N)>0$ such that \begin{align} \lim_{N\to\infty}\varepsilon_1 \left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{N}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\varepsilon_2 \,{N}=0. \end{align} The functions $F_1:\Omega_R\to\mathbb{R}$ and $F_2:\Gamma_r\to\mathbb{R}$, $r<R$, are supposed to be such that a unique solution $U$ of \eqref{eqn:11}--\eqref{eqn:13} exists and that the restriction $U^+$ is of class $\mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, for some fixed $s\geq 2$. The erroneous input data is given by $F_1^{\eps_1}=F_1+\eps_1 E_1$ and $F_2^{\eps_2}=F_2+\eps_2 E_2$, with $E_1\in L^2(\Omega_R)$ and $E_2\in L^2(\Omega_r)$. If the kernels $\Phi_N\in\textnormal{Pol}_{N}$ and kernel $\tilde{\Psi}_N\in\textnormal{Pol}_{ \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}$ are the minimizers of the functional $\mathcal{F}$ from \eqref{eqn:mineq2} and if $U_N^\eps$ is given as in \eqref{eqn:firstapprox3}, then \begin{align} \lim_{N\to\infty}\left\|U^+-U_ {N}^{\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^2(\tilde{\Gamma}_r)}=0. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Under a parameter-balance condition and coupled noise decay, the optimized two-step approximation converges to the true potential in $L^2(\tilde{\Gamma}_r)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.5 (asymptotically optimal localization of $\tilde{\Psi}_N$)
nodes.statement: Assume that the parameters $\alpha_{N,n}$, $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$, and $\beta_N$ are positive and suppose that, for some fixed $\delta>0$ and $\kappa>1$, \begin{align} \inf_{n=0,\ldots, \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\frac{\beta_N\frac{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2(N+1)}}{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^2}+( \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor+1)^2}{{\alpha}_{N,n}}&=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-2(1+\delta)}\right),\quad \textit{ for }N\to\infty. \end{align} The same relation shall hold true for $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$. Operators and kernels with a tilde mean that information is mapped from $\Gamma_r$ to $\Gamma_r$ while a lack of the tilde typically indicates the mapping of information from $\Omega_R$ to $\Omega_r$ (or $\Gamma_r$, respectively).

nodes.name: Remark 4.4 (relaxing $s\geq2$ via filtered kernels)
nodes.statement: The condition $U^+\in \mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s\geq 2$, in Theorem \ref{thm:convres} can be relaxed to $U^+\in \mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s>0$, if the minimizing functional $\mathcal{F}$ in \eqref{eqn:mineq2} is substituted by \begin{align} \mathcal{F}_{Filter}(\Phi_N,\tilde{\Psi}_N)=&\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor}\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\big|K_N^\wedge(n)-\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\big|^2+\sum_{n=0}^{N}\alpha_{N,n}\big|K_N^\wedge(n)-{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\sigma_n\big|^2 \\&+\beta_N\sum_{n=0}^{N}\big|\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\big|^2+8\pi^2 r^4\left\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\right\|^2_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])},\nonumber \end{align} where $K_N^\wedge(n)$ are the symbols of a filtered kernel (compare, e.g., \cite{yuguang132} and references therein for more information) \begin{align} \tilde{\Phi}_{N}^{Filter}(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}K_N^\wedge(n)Y_{n,k}\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right)Y_{n,k}\left(\frac{y}{|y|}\right). \end{align} Then the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:convres} follows in a very similar manner as before, just that the minimizing kernels are not compared to the Shannon-type kernel but to the filtered kernel. Opposed to the Shannon-type kernel, an appropriately filtered kernel has the localization property $\lim_{N\to\infty}\|\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^{Filter}\|_{L^1([-1,1-\rho])}=0$  which makes the condition $s\geq 2$ on the smoothness of $U^+$ (required for Proposition \ref{prop:loc1}) obsolete.
nodes.statement_short: Comparing to a filtered kernel instead of the Shannon kernel weakens the smoothness requirement from $s\geq2$ to $s>0$.

nodes.name: Discussion of the localization measure for $\tilde{\Psi}_N$
nodes.statement: However, using \eqref{eqn:altloc} as a penalty term in the functional $\mathcal{F}$ from \eqref{eqn:mineq2} would make it significantly harder to find its minimizers. Furthermore, it turns out that the kernel $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ that minimizes the original functional actually keeps the quantity \eqref{eqn:altloc} small as well (at least asymptotically in the sense that \eqref{eqn:altloc} vanishes for $N\to\infty$). The latter essentially originates from the property that $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ converges to a Shannon-type kernel (which has the desired property).
nodes.statement_short: The Slepian ratio is harder to minimize directly, but the optimized kernel keeps it small anyway because it converges to a Shannon-type kernel.

nodes.name: Remark 5.1 (parameter magnitudes vs. condition (4.1))
nodes.statement: Condition \eqref{eqn:ass1} suggests that the parameter $\beta_N$ should be significantly smaller than $\alpha_{N,n}$ and $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$. This does not seem to be reflected by the parameters in Tables \ref{tab:err1} and \ref{tab:err2}. But Condition \eqref{eqn:propx} implies a relation between $N$ and $\eps_1$, $\eps_2$ that, for the choice $N=100$, leads to significantly smaller $\eps_1$, $\eps_2$ than those chosen in Tables \ref{tab:err1} and \ref{tab:err2}. Indeed, if we choose, e.g., $\eps_1=\eps_2=10^{-10}$  and repeat the above examples for $\rho=0.5$, we obtain a set of good parameters $\beta_N=10^{-6}$, $\alpha_{N,n}=10^4$, $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}=10^4$ that reflects the expected behaviour. However, our goal was to test realistic noise levels for the intended applications and show that the proposed method via optimized kernels works well for these scenarios.
nodes.statement_short: The empirically best parameters contradict the asymptotic condition only because realistic noise levels are far from the asymptotic regime.

nodes.name: Remark 6.1 (choice of vector spherical harmonic basis)
nodes.statement: In geomagnetic modeling, another set of vector spherical harmonics is used more commonly than the one applied in this paper. We have used the basis \eqref{eqn:ynk1}--\eqref{eqn:ynk3} since it is generated by simpler differential operators, which reduces the effort to obtain a vectorial version of the localization principle later on. However, both basis systems eventually yield the same results. More information on the other basis system and its application in geomagnetism can be found, e.g., in \cite{backus96}, \cite{ger11}, \cite{ger12}, \cite{gubbins12}, and \cite{mayer06}.
nodes.statement_short: The chosen vector spherical harmonic basis is simpler for the localization proof but equivalent to the usual geomagnetic basis.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: The combination of satellite and ground data is an important step to obtain high-resolution models, e.g., of the Earth's gravitational and crustal magnetic field. The numerical examples in this article have shown that the proposed approach via optimized kernels yields improved results over a naive approximation by Shannon-type kernels. Furthermore, it proved superior to spline approximation/interpolation from ground data in $\Gamma_r$ and downward continuation of satellite data on $\Omega_R$ via TSVD/RCM over a wide range of scenarios. Splines can only compete if the noise level in $\Gamma_r$ is not larger than the noise level on $\Omega_R$. Downward continuation, on the other hand, is comparable only if the noise level on $\Omega_R$ is significantly smaller than in $\Gamma_r$. The combined approach presented here automatically weighs the different properties of ground and satellite data against each other. In this sense, a crucial ingredient for the construction of the optimized kernels is the choice of the parameters $\beta_N$, $\alpha_{N,n}$, $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}$, and the truncation degree $N$. They may be motivated by a priori knowledge of the noise levels $\eps_1$, $\eps_2$, and the size of the region $\Gamma_r$, but in general they will require an adequate yet to investigate parameter choice strategy.
nodes.statement_short: Optimized kernels beat Shannon kernels, splines, and TSVD/RCM across scenarios; a principled parameter-choice strategy remains open.

nodes.name: Two-step algorithm: downward continuation with $\Phi_N$ then local refinement with $\tilde{\Psi}_N$
nodes.statement: The approximation is based on a two-step algorithm motivated by spherical multiscale expansions: First, a convolution with a scaling kernel $\Phi_N$ deals with the downward continuation from $\Omega_R$ to $\Omega_r$, while in a second step, the result is locally refined by a convolution on $\Omega_r$ with a wavelet kernel $\tilde{\Psi}_N$. The kernels $\Phi_N$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N$ are optimized in such a way that the former behaves well for the downward continuation while the latter shows a good localization in $\Gamma_r$.
nodes.statement_short: Downward-continue global satellite data by a scaling convolution, then refine locally by a wavelet convolution of ground data, with both kernels jointly optimized.
input: globally available data on a sphere $\Omega_R$ of radius $R$ (e.g., a satellite's orbit)
locally available data in a subregion $\Gamma_r$ of the sphere $\Omega_r$ of radius $r<R$ (e.g., the spherical Earth's surface)

nodes.name: Step 1: scaling convolution for downward continuation
nodes.statement: First, a convolution with a scaling kernel $\Phi_N$ deals with the downward continuation from $\Omega_R$ to $\Omega_r$
nodes.statement_short: Convolve the satellite data with $\Phi_N$ to obtain a regularized downward continuation onto $\Omega_r$.

nodes.name: Step 2: local wavelet refinement
nodes.statement: while in a second step, the result is locally refined by a convolution on $\Omega_r$ with a wavelet kernel $\tilde{\Psi}_N$
nodes.statement_short: Add a wavelet convolution of the local ground data to refine the first-step result.

nodes.name: spherical splines (baseline from ground data only)
nodes.statement: spherical splines (based on the iterated Green function for the Beltrami operator; see, e.g., \cite{freeden81} and \cite{freeschrei09}) are applied for the approximation from local/regional data in $\Gamma_r$; for spherical cap radius $\rho=0.5$, we interpolate; for spherical cap radius $\rho=0.02$, we use a least square approach with smoothing parameter $\alpha=10^{-5}$ in order to deal with the ill-conditioned spline matrix (instead of a Gauss-Legendre grid, we choose approximately 30000 points in $\Gamma_r$ with similar spacing in longitudinal and latitudinal direction, avoiding concentration towards the poles and leading to better results for the spline method)
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: harmonic spline interpolation (or smoothed least squares) from ground data in $\Gamma_r$ only.
output: the approximation from local/regional data in $\Gamma_r$

nodes.name: truncated singular value decomposition (TSVD)
nodes.statement: when using satellite data on $\Omega_R$ only, we apply the truncated singular value decomposition (TSVD) for different cut-off degrees $M\in\{0,2,4,\ldots,100\}$
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: pure downward continuation of satellite data by spectral truncation at degree $M$.

nodes.name: regularized collocation method (RCM)
nodes.statement: in addition, the regularized collocation method (RCM) from \cite{naumov} with Tikhonov regularization is tested for different regularization parameters $\alpha\in\{10^{-7},\ldots,10^{-1}\}$ (the equiangular integration grid on $\Omega_R$ and the corresponding weights are the same as chosen before)
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: Tikhonov-regularized collocation for downward continuation of satellite data.

nodes.name: Numerical test with synthetic band-limited potential
nodes.statement: We generate a potential $U^+$ and data $F_1$, $F_2$ from uniformly distributed random Fourier coefficients up to spherical harmonic degree $100$. Analogously, the noise $E_1$, $E_2$ is produced by uniformly distributed random Fourier coefficients up to spherical harmonic degree $110$ and is then scaled such that $\|E_1\|_{L^2(\Omega_R)}=\|F_1\|_{L^2(\Omega_R)}$ and $\|E_2\|_{L^2(\Gamma_r)}=\|F_2\|_{L^2(\Gamma_r)}$. The mean Earth radius is given by $r=6371.2$km; for the satellite orbit we choose $R=7071.2$km (i.e., a satellite altitude of $700$km above the Earth's surface). We fix $N=100$ for the approximation $U_N^\varepsilon$ and choose $\kappa>0$ such that $\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor=130$. Then $U_N^\varepsilon$ is computed for the following different settings: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] data $F_1^{\varepsilon_1}$ is available on an equiangular grid of $40804$ points on $\Omega_R$; data $F_2^{\varepsilon_2}$ is given on a Gauss-Legendre grid of $49062$ points in a spherical cap $\Gamma_r=\mathcal{C}_r(x_0,2\rho)$ around the North pole $x_0$. We choose $\tilde{\Gamma}_r=\mathcal{C}_r(x_0,\rho)$ and vary the radius $\rho\in\{0.5,0.02\}$, \item[(b)] the parameters of the functional $\mathcal{F}$ are chosen among the cases $\beta_N\in\{10^{-3},\ldots,10^{4}\}$, $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\in\{10^{1},\ldots, 10^{8}\}$, as well as ${\alpha}_{N,n}\in\{\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n},0.2\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\}$, \item[(c)] the noise level on $\Omega_R$ is varied among $\varepsilon_1\in\{0.001,0.01,0.05,0.1\}$; for the noise in $\Gamma_r$ we choose $\varepsilon_2\in\{\varepsilon_1,2\varepsilon_1,5\varepsilon_1\}$. \end{itemize} For the numerical integration required for the evaluation of $U_N^\varepsilon$ we use the scheme from \cite{drihea} on $\Omega_R$ and the scheme from \cite{womers12} in $\mathcal{C}_r(x,\rho)$.
nodes.statement_short: Synthetic degree-100 potential with 100% relative noise, Earth/satellite radii $6371.2$/$7071.2$ km, $N=100$, $\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor=130$, caps of radius $\rho\in\{0.5,0.02\}$.

nodes.name: Observation (2): smoother transition between ground and satellite data
nodes.statement: The results in Table \ref{tab:err1} indicate the expected behaviour for the Shannon-type kernels: in the case $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ only ground data is used (i.e., cut-off degree $M=0$), while the cut-off degree increases if the noise level of the ground data in $\Gamma_r$ is larger than for the satellite data on $\Omega_R$ (i.e., $\varepsilon_2>\varepsilon_1$). The same behaviour can be observed for the optimized kernels (cf. Figure \ref{fig:kernelplot}(a)), however, with a smoother transition between ground and satellite data: e.g., for the choice $\beta_n=3\cdot 10^3$, $\tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}=10^3$, ${\alpha}_{N,n}=10^3$, mostly ground data is used (i.e., $\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)\approx 1$), but to a small extent (up to around spherical harmonic degree $n=10$) also satellite data is included (i.e., ${\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)\not=0$). This leads to an improvement of the relative error, e.g., by more than a factor two for the case $\eps_1=\eps_2=0.001$ (cf. Table \ref{tab:err1}(a)).
nodes.statement_short: Optimized kernels reproduce the expected noise-dependent weighting but blend satellite and ground data smoothly, halving the error at $\eps_1=\eps_2=0.001$.

nodes.name: Observation (3): small cap radius amplifies the error at low noise

Thus, the approximation error for small noise levels can be in first place accounted to an insufficient localization of the used kernels. Increasing the truncation degree $N$ of the scaling and wavelet kernels $\Phi_N$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N$, respectively, according to the size of the region $\Gamma_r$ (i.e., according to the radius $\rho$) can compensate this problem.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement_short: Compare the optimal functional value with the Shannon-type kernel value to get $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1-\delta})$ symbol rates, then kill the five terms of the error estimate one by one using Young's inequality and the Riemann localization property.

nodes.name: Introduce the auxiliary Shannon-type kernels
nodes.statement: As an auxiliary set of kernels, we define the Shannon-type kernels $\Phi_N^{Sh}$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}$ via the symbols \begin{align} \big(\Phi_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{1}{\sigma_n},&n\leq N,\\0,&\textnormal{else},\end{array}\right.\qquad \big(\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}1,&n\leq \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor,\\0,&\textnormal{else},\end{array}\right. \end{align} and $\big(\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)=\big(\tilde{\Phi}_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)-\big(\Phi_N^{Sh}\big)^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the TSVD/Shannon comparison kernels.

nodes.name: Bound $\mathcal{F}$ at the Shannon-type kernels
nodes.statement: By using the addition theorem for spherical harmonics and properties of the Legendre polynomials, we obtain \begin{align} \mathcal{F}(\Phi_N^{Sh},\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh})&=\beta_N\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{1}{\sigma_n^2}+8\pi^2 r^4\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}\big\|^2_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])} \\&\leq \beta_N\frac{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2(N+1)}}{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2}}+8\pi^2\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\left(\frac{2n+1}{4\pi}\right)^2\left\|P_n\right\|^2_{L^2([-1,1])}\nonumber \\&= \beta_N\frac{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2(N+1)}}{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2}}+(\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor+1)^2.\nonumber \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the functional at the Shannon kernels and bound it by the quantity appearing in condition (4.1).

nodes.name: Derive the $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1-\delta})$ symbol rates and kill the first two error terms
nodes.statement: The kernels that minimize $\mathcal{F}$ are denoted by $\Phi_N$ and $\tilde{\Psi}_N$. In consequence, \begin{align} \tilde{\alpha}_{N,n}\big(1-\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\big)^2&\leq\mathcal{F}(\Phi_N,\tilde{\Psi}_N)\leq \mathcal{F}(\Phi_N^{Sh},\tilde{\Psi}_N^{Sh}) \\&\leq \beta_N\frac{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2(N+1)}}{1-\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{2}}+(\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor+1)^2,\nonumber \end{align} for all $n\leq \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$. In combination with \eqref{eqn:ass1}, this leads to \begin{align} \big|1-\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)\big|= \mathcal{O}(N^{-1-\delta}), \end{align} uniformly for all $n\leq \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$ and $N\to\infty$. The estimate $|1-\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1-\delta})$ follows in the same manner and holds uniformly for all $n\leq N$ and $N\to\infty$. Finally, since $\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)=0$ for $n> \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$, we end up with \begin{align} \lim_{N\to\infty}\sup_{n=0,1,\ldots}\frac{|1-\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)|}{(n+\frac{1}{2})^{s}}=0, \end{align} which shows that the first term on the right hand side of the error estimate \eqref{eqn:errorestfinal} vanishes. The second term can be treated analogously.
nodes.statement_short: Optimality plus condition (4.1) forces the symbols to approach 1 at rate $N^{-1-\delta}$, killing the two approximation terms.

nodes.name: Third error term: satellite noise amplification vanishes
nodes.statement: Due to the uniform boundedness of $|\Phi_J^\wedge(n)\sigma_n|$, there exists some constant $C>0$ such that \eqref{eqn:propx} implies \begin{align} \lim_{N\to\infty}\eps_1\sup_{n=0,1,\ldots}\left|\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\right|\leq C\lim_{N\to\infty}\eps_1\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{N}=0. \end{align} so that the third term on the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:errorestfinal} vanishes as well.
nodes.statement_short: The noise-decay coupling $\eps_1(R/r)^N\to0$ controls the amplified satellite noise.

nodes.name: Fourth error term: refine the estimate instead of the supremum
nodes.statement: The fourth term does not vanish. However, taking a closer look at the derivation of this term, we see that it suffices to show that $\big\|\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\tilde{\Psi}_{N}^\wedge(n)F_r^\wedge(n,k)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\big\|_{L^2(\Omega_r)}$ tends to zero (where $F$ stands for $U^+$ or $E_2$). Using the previous results and $|\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|\leq |1-{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n|+|1-\tilde{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)|$, it follows that \begin{align} \left\|\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\tilde{\Psi}_{N}^\wedge(n)F_r^\wedge(n,k)\frac{1}{r}Y_{n,k}\right\|_{L^2(\Omega_r)}^2\leq \mathcal{O}(N^{-2\delta})+C\sum_{n=N+1}^{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor}\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\left|F_r^\wedge(n,k)\right|^2, \end{align} for some constant $C>0$. Latter vanishes for $N\to\infty$ since $F$ (i.e., $U^+$ or $E_2$) is of class $L^2(\Omega_r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the non-vanishing supremum by the actual $L^2$ tail, which vanishes by square-summability.

nodes.name: Last error term: split against the Shannon kernel and apply the localization property
nodes.statement: In order to handle the last term of the error estimate \eqref{eqn:errorestfinal}, it has to be shown that $\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}$ tends to zero. This, again, is generally not true. But, taking a closer look at the derivation of the estimate indicates that it suffices to show that \small\begin{align} \Bigg\|\,\,\int_{\Omega_r\setminus\mathcal{C}_r(\rho,\cdot)}\tilde{\Psi}_{N}(\cdot,y) U^+(y)d\omega(y)\Bigg\|_{L^2(\Omega_r)}, \qquad \eps_2\Bigg\|\,\,\int_{\Omega_r\setminus\mathcal{C}_r(\rho,\cdot)}\tilde{\Psi}_{N}(\cdot,y) E_2(y)d\omega(y)\Bigg\|_{L^2(\Omega_r)} \end{align}\normalsize vanish as $N\to\infty$. [...] where Young's inequality has been used in the last row. Since $U^+\in \mathcal{H}_s(\Omega_r)$, $s\geq 2$, Proposition \ref{prop:loc1} implies that the first term on the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:locest} tends to zero as $N\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the leakage integral into a Shannon part (handled by Proposition 4.2) and a difference part (handled by Young's inequality).

nodes.name: Bound the kernel difference and combine all steps
nodes.statement: The second term on the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:locest} can be treated as follows \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\big\|\tilde{\Psi}^{Sh}_{N}-\tilde{\Psi}_{N}\big\|_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}^2 \\&\leq\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\left(\frac{2n+1}{4\pi}\right)^2\left|\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)-\left(\tilde{\Psi}^{Sh}_N\right)^\wedge(n)\right|^2\|P_n\|_{L^2([-1,1])}^2 \\&\leq\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\frac{2n+1}{8\pi^2}\left|\left|\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)-1\right|+\left|{\Phi}_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n-1\right|\chi_{[0,N]}(n)\right|^2 \\&=\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\frac{2n+1}{8\pi^2}\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-2(1+\delta)}\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-2\delta}\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} By $\chi_{[0,N]}(n)$ we mean the characteristic function, i.e., it is equal to 1 if $n=0,\ldots,N$, and equal to 0 otherwise. In conclusion, the left expression in \eqref{eqn:altterms} vanishes as $N\to\infty$. For the right expression in \eqref{eqn:altterms}, we obtain the desired result in a similar but easier manner. Finally, combining all steps of the proof, we have shown that the right hand side of the error estimate \eqref{eqn:errorestfinal} converges to zero, which yields \eqref{eqn:convres}.
nodes.statement_short: The optimized kernel converges to the Shannon kernel at rate $\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta})$, so every term of the error estimate vanishes.

nodes.statement:
The function $F_N(t)={|	ilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2}/{\|	ilde{\Psi}_N\|^2_{L^2([-1,1])}}$ can be regarded as the density function of a random variable $t\in[-1,1]$. By $P_N(t< a)$ we mean the probability (with respect to the density function $F_N$) that $t$ lies in the interval $[-1,a)$ while $P_N(t\geq a)$ means the probability of $t$ being in the interval $[a,1]$. onumber \end{align} From \eqref{eqn:conphij} and the corresponding estimate for $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$ we find $|	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|^2=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2(1+\delta)})$ for $n\leq N$, and $|1-	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|^2=|1-	ilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)|^2=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2(1+\delta)})$, for $N+1\leq n\leq \lfloor\kappa Nfloor$. As a consequence,  \eqref{eqn:et1} implies  egin{align} &\int_{-1}^1 t|	ilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2 dt \&=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2\delta})+\sum_{n=N+1}^{\lfloor\kappa Nfloor}  rac{2n+1}{8\pi^2r^2}|	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|^2\left( rac{n}{2n+1} rac{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n-1)}{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)}+ rac{n+1}{2n+1} rac{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n+1)}{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)}ight),
onumber \end{align} where $\sup_{N+1\leq n\leq\lfloor \kappa Nfloor} ig|1- ig( rac{n}{2n+1}{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n-1)}/{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)}+ rac{n+1}{2n+1}{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n+1)}/{	ilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)} ig) ig|\leq\varepsilon_N$, for  some $\varepsilon_N>0$ that satisfies $\varepsilon_N	o0$ as $N	o\infty$. nodes.name: Reduce to mean and variance via Cantelli's inequality
nodes.statement: The function $F_N(t)={|\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2}/{\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\|^2_{L^2([-1,1])}}$ can be regarded as the density function of a random variable $t\in[-1,1]$. Thus, we can write \begin{align} \frac{\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\big\|^2_{L^2([-1,1-\rho])}}{\big\|\tilde{\Psi}_N\big\|^2_{L^2([-1,1])}}&=\int_{-1}^{1-\rho}F_N(t)dt=P_N(t< 1-\rho)=1-P_N\big(t-E_N(t)\geq 1-\rho-E_N(t)\big)\nonumber \\&\leq \frac{V_N(t)}{V_N(t)+ (1-\rho-E_N(t))^2}, \end{align} where we have used Cantelli's inequality for the last estimate. nodes.statement: First, we use the addition theorem for spherical harmonics and the recurrence relation $tP_n(t)=\frac{1}{2n+1}\left((n+1)P_{n+1}(t)+nP_{n-1}(t)\right)$ to obtain \begin{align} \int_{-1}^1 t|\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2 dt&= \frac{1}{r^2} \sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\sum_{m=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}\frac{2n+1}{4\pi}\frac{2m+1}{4\pi}\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(m)\int_{-1}^1tP_n(t)P_m(t)dt [...] \\&=\frac{1}{8\pi^2r^2}\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor}n\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n-1)+(n+1)\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n+1).\nonumber \end{align}

nodes.name: Insert the symbol rates from the proof of Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement: From \eqref{eqn:conphij} and the corresponding estimate for $\Phi_N^\wedge(n)\sigma_n$ we find $|\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|^2=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2(1+\delta)})$ for $n\leq N$, and $|1-\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|^2=|1-\tilde{\Phi}_{N}^\wedge(n)|^2=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2(1+\delta)})$, for $N+1\leq n\leq \lfloor\kappa N\rfloor$. As a consequence,  \eqref{eqn:et1} implies \begin{align} &\int_{-1}^1 t|\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2 dt \\&=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2\delta})+\sum_{n=N+1}^{\lfloor\kappa N\rfloor} \frac{2n+1}{8\pi^2r^2}|\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)|^2\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\frac{\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n-1)}{\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)}+\frac{n+1}{2n+1}\frac{\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n+1)}{\tilde{\Psi}_N^\wedge(n)}\right),\nonumber \end{align}

Together with  egin{align} \|	ilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\|_{L^2([-1,1])}^2=\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor \kappa Nfloor}  rac{2n+1}{4\pi^2r^2}|	ilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)|^2=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2\delta})+\sum_{n=N+1}^{\lfloor \kappa Nfloor}  rac{2n+1}{4\pi^2r^2}|	ilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)|^2, \end{align} this leads to the desired property  egin{align} \lim_{N	o\infty}E_N(t)=\lim_{N	o\infty}\int_{-1}^1 t|F_N(t)|^2 dt=\lim_{N	o\infty} rac{\int_{-1}^1 t|	ilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2 dt}{\|	ilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\|_{L^2([-1,1])}^2}=1, \end{align} concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Same probabilistic scheme as Lemma 4.5, but the type-2 moment requires Green's formulas and surface-Laplacian identities before reducing to a one-dimensional Legendre integral.

nodes.name: Set up the tensor-zonal density and reduce to moments
nodes.statement: Set $F_N(t)={|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N(x,y)|^2}/{\|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\|^2_{L^2([-1,1])}}$, where $t=\xi \cdot\eta $. Since $\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N$ is tensor-zonal, $F_N$ is well-defined and can be regarded as a density function of a random variable $t\in[-1,1]$. From here on, the proof is essentially the same as for Lemma \ref{lem:loc} and we have to show $\lim_{N\to\infty}E_N(t)=1$ and $\lim_{N\to\infty}V_N(t)=0$. We just indicate the proof for $E_N(t)$, the case of $V_N(t)$ follows analogously.
nodes.statement_short: Tensor-zonality makes the normalized squared kernel a density; reduce again to mean and variance.

nodes.name: Expand the first moment into type-1 and type-2 contributions
nodes.statement: Setting $\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)=|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N(x,y)|$, again with $t=\xi \cdot\eta $, we get \begin{align} &2\pi r^2\int_{-1}^1t|\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2dt=\int_{\Omega_r}\xi \cdot\eta \left|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\left(r\xi ,r\eta \right)\right|^2d\omega(r\eta) [...] \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Write the first moment as a spherical integral of the squared tensorial kernel and split by type.

nodes.name: Reduce the first term to a one-dimensional Legendre integral
nodes.statement: The first term on the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:ejtvect} can be written as a one-dimensional integral \begin{align} [...] &=\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor}\sum_{m=0}^{{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor}}\frac{(2n+1)(2m+1)}{8\pi}\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(m)\int_{-1}^1tP_{n}\left(t\right)P_{m}\left(t\right)dt.\nonumber \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The radial-type term collapses to $\int_{-1}^1 tP_nP_m$ by the addition theorem.

nodes.name: Green's formula for the surface-gradient integral
nodes.statement:
The second term requires significantly more effort. We start by observing that  egin{align} &\int_{\Omega_r}\eta \left(
abla^*_{\eta }Y_{n,k}\left(\eta ight)\cdot
abla^*_{\eta }Y_{m,l}\left(\eta ight)ight)d\omega(r\eta) [...] \&= rac{n(n+1)}{2}\int_{\Omega_r}\eta Y_{n,k}\left(\eta ight)Y_{m,l}\left(\eta ight)d\omega(r\eta)
onumber + rac{m(m+1)}{2}\int_{\Omega_r}\eta Y_{n,k}\left(\eta ight)Y_{m,l}\left(\eta ight)d\omega(r\eta),
onumber \end{align} where we have used $
abla_{\eta}^*\cdot\left(\eta\otimes
abla^*_{\eta}Y_{n,k}\left(\etaight)ight)=\eta\Delta_\eta^*Y_{n,k}\left(\etaight)+
abla_\eta^*Y_{n,k}\left(\etaight)$.
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts converts the surface-gradient product into eigenvalue-weighted products of spherical harmonics.

nodes.name: Evaluate the second term
nodes.statement:
Plugging \eqref{eqn:1green} into the second term on the right hand side of Equation \eqref{eqn:ejtvect}, and using the expression $2
abla_\xi ^*Y_{n,k}(\xi )\cdot 
abla_\xi ^*Y_{m,l}(\xi )=\Delta_\xi ^*(Y_{n,k}(\xi )Y_{m,l}(\xi ))+(n(n+1)+m(m+1))Y_{n,k}(\xi )Y_{m,l}(\xi )$, leads to  egin{align} [...] &=\sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor \kappa Nfloor}\sum_{m=1}^{{\lfloor \kappa Nfloor}}	ilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)	ilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(m)\left( rac{1}{2}+ rac{n(n+1)-2}{2m(m+1)}ight) rac{(2n+1)(2m+1)}{8\pi}\int_{-1}^1tP_n(t)P_m(t)dt,
onumber \end{align} where we have used the addition theorem, the property $\Delta_{\xi }^*P_n(\xi \cdot\eta)=\Delta_{\eta}^*P_n(\xi \cdot\eta)$, Green's formulas, and $\Delta_{\eta}^*\,\eta=-2\eta$ in the last row.
nodes.statement_short: The tangential-type term also reduces to a weighted one-dimensional Legendre integral.

nodes.name: Combine both terms into a single moment formula
nodes.statement: Eventually, combining \eqref{eqn:ejtvect}, \eqref{eqn:firstsum}, and \eqref{eqn:2term}, we are lead to \begin{align} &\int_{-1}^1t|\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2dt \\&=\sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor}\sum_{m=1}^{{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor}}\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(m)\left(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{n(n+1)-2}{4m(m+1)}\right)\frac{(2n+1)(2m+1)}{8\pi^2r^2}\int_{-1}^1tP_n(t)P_m(t)dt.\nonumber \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Both contributions merge into one weighted double sum for the first moment.

nodes.name: Conclude $E_N(t)\to1$ as in the scalar case
nodes.statement: Observing $\lim_{m,n\to\infty}\frac{3}{4}+\frac{n(n+1)-2}{4m(m+1)}=1$ if $m\in\{n-1,n,n+1\}$, we can proceed with \eqref{eqn:inttpsiN} in a similar manner as in  \eqref{eqn:et1} and \eqref{eqn:et11}. Together with \begin{align} \|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\|_{L^2([-1,1])}^2=\sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor} \frac{2n+1}{4\pi^2r^2}|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)|^2=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2\delta})+\sum_{n=N+1}^{\lfloor \kappa N\rfloor} \frac{2n+1}{4\pi^2r^2}|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N^\wedge(n)|^2, \end{align} this leads to the desired property \begin{align} \lim_{N\to\infty}E_N(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_{-1}^1 t|F_N(t)|^2 dt=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\int_{-1}^1 t|\tilde{\Psi}_N(t)|^2 dt}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{\Psi}}_N\|_{L^2([-1,1])}^2}=1, \end{align} concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The weight tends to 1 on the diagonal band, so the mean tends to 1 exactly as in Lemma 4.5.
